title: Chandaka sent back
hookLine: the charioteer begs to stay; the prince sends him home with his jewels (Buddhacarita 6)

cards: Sunrise, and a horse that has run all night stands blowing at the edge of a hermitage. A young man climbs down. For the first time in his life, there is no palace behind him.
Beside him stands Chandaka, the attendant who saddled the horse in the dark and rode out with him. He has done everything he was told all night. Now the prince gives him one more order: go home.

teach.b: First, the thanks. Before any parting, the prince praises Chandaka: this loyalty, he says in paraphrase, is rare, a man who follows his master when there is nothing to gain by it.

Second, the jewels. He takes off his ornaments and puts them in Chandaka's hands, with a message for the king. Tell my father I haven't gone into the forest out of anger, or for lack of love, or out of longing for heaven.
I've gone to put an end to old age and death. Don't grieve for me. Third, the begging.
Chandaka weeps. How can I lead this horse home with an empty saddle? What do I say to your father, to the queen who raised you, to your wife?

teach.h: BIRDS IN ONE TREE FOR A NIGHT.
teach.b: The prince answers gently, with an image from the poem: beings meet the way birds gather in one tree for the night, and in the morning they fly off in different directions.
Parting comes for everyone; this one, at least, has a purpose. Fourth, the last things.

With his own sword the prince cuts off his long hair. A hunter in a dull-colored robe passes by, and the prince trades his fine silk clothes for that plain cloth; the poem says the hunter was a god in disguise.
Then Chandaka turns for home, slowly, leading Kanthaka, and the poem says the horse licked the prince's feet and wept before he went.
Since the old man on the cleared road, the poem has been taking things from the prince one at a time: his ease, a garden's charm, a friend's good argument, the palace.
Today it's the jewels, his hair, his clothes and his last companion, and each one goes back with care.

how: The cutting of the hair and the change into a plain robe are remembered in Buddhist ordinations, where in some communities a new monk or nun has the head shaved and puts on the robe before taking vows.

games.q: the parting at the forest's edge: tap the pairs.

s: in the poem, the prince tells the king he left out of anger
his message says he left not from anger or lack of love, but to end old age and death.
Chandaka goes home gladly when he's told to
he weeps and begs to stay; the prince has to answer him first.
the prince cuts his own hair with his sword

games.q: you're Chandaka. you've ridden all night beside the prince, and at sunrise he puts his jewels in your hands and tells you to go home. what do you do?
o: weep and beg to stay with him.
pretend to leave, then follow him.
games.why: he weeps and pleads: how can he bring the horse home with an empty saddle? the prince answers that beings meet like birds in one tree for a night, then part, and sends him home.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you're holding that isn't really yours to keep: a borrowed book, a coat that hasn't left the closet in years, a job on a committee you agreed to long ago.
Picture giving it back the way the prince did, thanks first, then a clear word about why, then open hands. Let your hands rest open in your lap for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Chandaka. The prince's attendant, thanked and sent home from the forest's edge with the horse, the jewels, and a message for the king. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the name of the prince's attendant; Pali tellings call him Channa.

carryVoice: Your line: sent home with the jewels. Thanks first, then the honest reason. That's day seven hundred seven.

sources.ref: Buddhacarita 6 (Chandaka dismissed: the thanks, the jewels and message, the pleading, the hair and the robe)
